solutions.latex:
$f'(x)=12x^2-4x^3$, $f''(x)=24x-12x^2$

$f'(x)=0\Rightarrow12x^2-4x^3=0\Rightarrow4x^2(3-x)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=3$.

At $x=3$: $f''(3)=24\times3-12\times3^2=-36<0$, so a maximum at $x=3$. $f(3)=3+4\times3^3-3^4=30$, so $(3,30)$ is a point of maximum.

At $x=0$: $f''(x)=0$. Test concavity:

$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&-1&0&1\\\hline f''(x)&-36&0&12\end{array}$

The sign of $f''$ changes from negative to positive, so at $x=0$ there is a horizontal point of inflexion. $f(0)=3$, so $(0,3)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: stationary x-values; 1: nature of (3,30); 1: nature of (0,3)

solutions.latex:
$f''(x)=0\Rightarrow24x-12x^2=0\Rightarrow12x(2-x)=0\Rightarrow x=0$ or $x=2$.

When $x=0$ the curve has a horizontal point of inflexion (proved in part (a)).

When $x=2$:

$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&1&2&3\\\hline f''(x)&12&0&-36\end{array}$

The concavity changes, so there is a point of inflexion at $x=2$. $f(2)=3+4\times2^3-2^4=19$.

The curve has a point of inflexion at $(2,19)$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: shows f''=0 with change of concavity and y-value

solutions.latex:
$f'(x)=e^{2x}\times(-1)+(1-x)\times2e^{2x}=-e^{2x}+2e^{2x}-2xe^{2x}=e^{2x}(1-2x)$

$f'(x)=0$: $e^{2x}(1-2x)=0$. Since $e^{2x}>0$ for all $x$, $1-2x=0$, so $x=\dfrac12$.

When $x=\dfrac12$, $f\left(\tfrac12\right)=e^{1}\left(1-\tfrac12\right)=\dfrac e2$.

The curve has only one stationary point $\left(\dfrac12,\dfrac e2\right)$, or $\left(\dfrac12,1.36\right)$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: derivative; 1: sets derivative to zero and uses e^{2x}>0; 1: x = 1/2 only

solutions.latex:
$$f(-x)=\frac{2^{-x}-1}{2(2^{-x}+1)}=\frac{\frac1{2^x}-1}{2\left(\frac1{2^x}+1\right)}=\frac{1-2^x}{2(1+2^x)}=-\frac{2^x-1}{2(2^x+1)}=-f(x)$$

Therefore $f(x)$ is an odd function.

Alternative solution: multiply numerator and denominator of $f(-x)$ by $\dfrac{2^x}{2^x}$ to get $\dfrac{1-2^x}{2(1+2^x)}=-f(x)$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: finds f(-x) correctly; 1: concludes odd

Total fuel burnt in first 7 minutes $=\displaystyle\int_0^7R\,dt$

$$=5\Big[\left(2\times7+\ln|1+2\times7|\right)-\left(2\times0+\ln1\right)\Big]=5\left[14+\ln15\right]\text{ kg}$$

So the girls enter the lower cave at 10:53 am.

The wire is $5$ m long and the base $BC=x$, so $AC=5-x$.

$AB^2=(5-x)^2-x^2=25-10x+x^2-x^2=25-10x$

$AB=\sqrt{25-10x}$

solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: uses Pythagoras for AB; 1: area formula

solutions.latex:
$A=\dfrac12x\sqrt{25-10x}$

$$\frac{dA}{dx}=\frac12\left[1\times\sqrt{25-10x}+x\times\frac{-10}{2\sqrt{25-10x}}\right]=\frac12\left[\frac{25-10x-5x}{\sqrt{25-10x}}\right]=\frac12\times\frac{25-15x}{\sqrt{25-10x}}$$

$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0\Rightarrow25-15x=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{25}{15}=\dfrac53\approx1.67$

$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&1&\frac53&2\\\hline \frac{dA}{dx}&1.29&0&-1.12\end{array}$

$\dfrac{dA}{dx}$ changes sign from positive to negative, so $A$ is a maximum when $x=\dfrac53$.

Maximum area $=\dfrac12\times\dfrac53\times\sqrt{25-\dfrac{10\times5}{3}}=\dfrac56\sqrt{\dfrac{25}{3}}=\dfrac{25}{6\sqrt3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac{25\sqrt3}{18}$ square metres.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: derivative; 1: x = 5/3; 1: justifies maximum; 1: maximum area
